definition: The speed–accuracy tradeoff is the balance between how fast a person makes a perceptual decision and how accurate that decision is. In plain terms, greater time pressure can shift performance toward speed at the expense of accuracy, or toward accuracy with slower responding.

reasons: The packet supports that time pressure influences perceptual decisions and that speed–accuracy tradeoff (SAT) is a relevant concept, but it does not define SAT as a balance between speed and accuracy or state that greater time pressure shifts performance toward speed at the expense of accuracy.
The added plain-language explanation about trading off speed for accuracy is an unsupported generalization beyond the supplied source text.

The packet does not state the general principle that the speed–accuracy tradeoff is “the balance between how fast a person makes a perceptual decision and how accurate that decision is,” nor does it define SAT in that way; it only mentions that time pressure influences perceptual decisions and that SAT effects are poorly understood in a specific context (color discrimination).
The packet does not support the claim that “greater time pressure can shift performance toward speed at the expense of accuracy, or toward accuracy with slower responding.”
